name: Sorting network on 21 inputs
description: Construct a sorting network on 21 wires with as few comparators as possible. A comparator (i, j) with i < j compares the values on wires i and j and puts the smaller one on wire i and the larger one on wire j; the comparators are applied in the given order. The network must sort every input, that is, leave the values in non-decreasing order along wires 0 to 20.
contract: construct() -> list of comparators (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < 21, in the order in which they are applied (at least one). The network is verified on all 2^21 inputs of zeros and ones, which is equivalent to sorting every input. Score: number of comparators, minimized (the depth is not scored).
notes: Best known size 99 (Dobbelaere's list), proven lower bound 80 (the list withdrew its stronger bounds for 13 or more inputs on 2026-11-20 because of an error in a proof of Van Voorhis 1972; 80 is 39, the proven optimum for 12 inputs, plus ceil(log2 k) for each further input k).
The size-minimisation problem for sorting networks on 21 wires, from Dobbelaere's list of smallest known sorting networks.
Exact 0-1 verification over all 2^21 inputs, in blocks of 2^24.
SorterHunter and symmetry-based searches have worked on these sizes for years.

sources.locator: Using Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks

science_relevance.reason: Valsalam and Miikkulainen's main objective is the comparator count of sorting networks with up to 32 inputs, which is exactly what the task scores; the record itself comes from Dobbelaere's SorterHunter-based list, which is a web page and not a paper, so only one paper qualifies and the status rests on it.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Construct a sorting network on 21 wires with as few comparators as possible.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Sorting networks are oblivious sorting procedures used in hardware, SIMD and GPU sorting, and the minimum number of comparators is known only for up to 12 inputs; for 13 and more inputs the best known sizes are upper bounds that have been lowered by evolutionary and SAT searches, so a smaller network is a new upper bound.

papers.title: Using Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks
papers.task_relation: The paper treats the same size-minimisation problem up to 32 inputs: its Table 2 lists the then best known sizes for 17 to 32 inputs and its abstract reports new minimal networks for 17 to 22 inputs and ties for larger n. The task's 21-input records (Dobbelaere's list) are lower than the paper's for 19 to 29 inputs and equal for 30 to 32; the paper is not the source of the current record.
papers.primary_goal: Minimise the number of comparators of sorting networks with a method combining problem symmetry and evolutionary search (SENSO).
